blocks.content: Every millisecond of latency between a user and the data they are asking for is a millisecond the user actually feels. A single origin server, no matter how powerful, cannot get around one hard fact of physics: light, and therefore data, takes time to travel, and the further it travels, the slower a request feels. A Content Delivery Network, or CDN, is the answer distributed systems have converged on: instead of moving the data faster, move a copy of the data physically closer to the user in the first place.

This page walks through what a CDN actually does under the hood, how it decides where to route a request, what it can and cannot cache, and where its limits are, since a CDN is a form of caching, and everything you already know about caching from the rest of this section applies here too, just spread across an entire planet instead of one machine.
1. The Problem a CDN Solves
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281158822-114403542.png
blocks.alt: A user close to the origin server gets a fast response; a user on the other side of the world pays for every mile in between

blocks.content: Imagine a single origin server sitting in a data center in Virginia. A user in Virginia hits that server and gets a response in a few milliseconds. A user in Mumbai, sending the exact same request, pays the cost of a round trip that crosses oceans and continents, easily 200 to 300 milliseconds before a single byte of the actual response even starts arriving. No amount of optimizing the server itself fixes that, the delay is baked into the distance.

There is a second, related problem too: every single user on earth hitting one origin server concentrates all of that load onto one place. A traffic spike anywhere in the world becomes a traffic spike that one origin has to absorb alone.

This is not a small effect either. Industry data consistently shows that even a 100 millisecond increase in load time measurably hurts conversion rates and how long users stay engaged, which is exactly why every major consumer-facing company treats this problem as worth solving seriously rather than shrugging off as an acceptable cost of doing business globally.

The concentration problem is just as real as the latency one. A single origin serving every user on the planet has no choice but to scale itself to handle worldwide peak demand at all times, even though at any given moment most of that capacity sits idle somewhere while another region is under real load.
2. What a CDN Actually Is

A CDN is a large, globally distributed network of servers, called edge servers or points of presence (PoPs), each holding a cached copy of content that would otherwise have to be fetched from the origin every single time. A user request gets routed to whichever edge server is closest to them geographically (or, more precisely, closest in network terms, which is usually but not always the same thing), and if that edge already has the content cached, the origin server is never even contacted.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281160752-103098183.png
blocks.alt: The same origin content gets copied out to edge locations spread around the world, each one serving the users nearest to it

blocks.content: The effect is exactly what you would hope for: the user in Mumbai now talks to an edge server in Mumbai, not a server in Virginia, and the 200 millisecond cross-ocean trip simply disappears from their experience.

It is worth being precise about the terminology too: a PoP (point of presence) is a physical facility, often housing equipment from multiple providers, while an edge server specifically refers to the CDN provider machines within it. In casual conversation the two terms are frequently used interchangeably, which is fine, but knowing the distinction exists is useful when reading more technical documentation.

It is also worth noting a CDN edge is doing exactly the same cache-aside work covered earlier in this course, just running on hardware physically distributed around the world instead of sitting next to a single application server.
3. How a Request Finds Its Nearest Edge
blocks.text: 3. How a Request Finds Its Nearest Edge

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281163148-573347519.png
blocks.alt: The network itself, not the application, decides which edge is nearest and routes the request there automatically

blocks.content: This routing happens beneath the application layer entirely, usually through one of two mechanisms. DNS-based routing resolves the CDN domain to a different IP address depending on where the request is coming from, so a user in Mumbai and a user in London resolve the same hostname to two completely different edge servers. Anycast routing goes a level deeper, advertising the exact same IP address from every edge location simultaneously, and letting standard internet routing protocols naturally send each user packets to whichever advertiser is topologically closest. Either way, the application itself never has to know or care which specific edge served a given user, that decision is made entirely by the network.

Neither mechanism requires the application developer to write any routing logic at all, which is precisely the appeal, this entire layer of complexity is handled transparently by the CDN provider and the underlying internet infrastructure, not by application code.
3.1 Using more than one CDN
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028797-463434383.png
blocks.alt: Some organizations split traffic across two CDN providers, switching between them based on real-time performance

blocks.content: Larger organizations sometimes run a multi-CDN setup, splitting traffic across two or more CDN providers and dynamically routing based on real-time performance data, which provider is fastest for a given region right now, or as a safeguard against one provider having an outage. This adds real operational complexity, but for a business where even a few minutes of degraded delivery is expensive, that complexity is a reasonable trade.
4. Origin Pull vs Origin Push
There are two fundamentally different ways content ends up sitting on an edge server in the first place, and the difference matters for how fresh, and how complete, the edge cache actually is.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281167425-116963995.png
blocks.alt: On a pull CDN, the edge only fetches from the origin the first time a specific file is actually requested

blocks.content: Origin pull (sometimes called reactive caching) is the far more common model. The edge starts out empty, and the very first request for any given file causes a cache miss, the edge fetches it from the origin, caches it, and serves it, exactly the cache-aside pattern already familiar from earlier in this section, just running at the edge of the network instead of next to a database. Every subsequent request for that same file, from any user routed to that same edge, is served straight from the edge cache.

Origin push flips this around: content is proactively uploaded to every edge location ahead of time, before any user has ever asked for it. This suits content you know in advance will be popular everywhere, a major software release, a video premiere, rather than waiting for organic traffic to slowly populate each edge cache one cache miss at a time.

Most real deployments actually use pull as the default and reserve push for a small number of known, high-value assets. It is rarely worth the operational overhead of pre-uploading everything everywhere when the vast majority of content naturally becomes cached within seconds of its first real request anyway.
5. What Actually Gets Cached

Static content, images, videos, CSS and JavaScript bundles, PDFs, is the classic, easy case for a CDN. It does not change per user and does not change often, so caching it at the edge for hours or days is completely safe.

Dynamic content, a personalized dashboard, an API response tailored to one logged-in user, is much harder to cache safely, since caching the wrong user response and serving it to someone else is a serious bug, not just a staleness problem. Modern CDNs increasingly support caching dynamic content too, but only with careful attention to cache keys (including things like the user session or query parameters in what counts as a unique cache entry) and much shorter TTLs.

blocks.title: A useful rule of thumb
blocks.content: If the exact same response is correct for every single user who requests it, it is a strong candidate for CDN caching. The moment the response depends on who is asking, caching it safely gets meaningfully harder.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281169904-251337265.png
blocks.alt: Everything that could make two requests actually different needs to be part of the cache key, or they will wrongly share one cached response

blocks.content: The subtlety with dynamic content is the cache key, the set of request attributes that decide whether two requests are considered "the same" for caching purposes. Cache by URL alone, and a request for /product/42?currency=USD and one for /product/42?currency=INR would wrongly share a cache entry, showing one user prices in the wrong currency. Getting the cache key right means explicitly deciding which query parameters, headers, or cookies actually change the response, and including exactly those in the key, no more and no less.

["Images, video, and downloadable files: the easiest and most valuable case, identical for everyone, safe to cache for a long time.","CSS and JavaScript bundles: also safe to cache aggressively, especially when filenames include a content hash that changes automatically whenever the file itself changes.","API responses: cacheable only when genuinely identical across users, and only for as long as staleness is acceptable for that specific endpoint."]
items: Images, video, and downloadable files: the easiest and most valuable case, identical for everyone, safe to cache for a long time.
CSS and JavaScript bundles: also safe to cache aggressively, especially when filenames include a content hash that changes automatically whenever the file itself changes.
API responses: cacheable only when genuinely identical across users, and only for as long as staleness is acceptable for that specific endpoint.

blocks.content: 6. Cache-Control Headers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281171942-612811655.png
blocks.alt: The origin tells every downstream cache, including CDN edges, exactly how long a response is allowed to be reused

blocks.content: The origin server communicates caching rules to every edge (and every browser, for that matter) through the Cache-Control HTTP header, the same mechanism used for browser caching, just respected by CDN edges too.

Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400

# public       -> any cache, including shared CDN edges, may store this
# max-age=86400 -> keep it for 24 hours before checking with the origin again

code.content:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400

# public       -> any cache, including shared CDN edges, may store this
# max-age=86400 -> keep it for 24 hours before checking with the origin again

codes.text:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400

# public       -> any cache, including shared CDN edges, may store this
# max-age=86400 -> keep it for 24 hours before checking with the origin again

blocks.content: Getting this header right is, in practice, one of the most consequential decisions in using a CDN well. Too short a max-age and the CDN barely helps, every request nearly falls straight through to the origin. Too long, and a fix or update takes an uncomfortably long time to actually reach users.
6.1 A quick reference

Beyond max-age, a few other Cache-Control directives come up often: no-store tells every cache, including the browser, never to keep a copy at all, appropriate for anything sensitive. must-revalidate forces a check with the origin once the max-age has expired, rather than optimistically continuing to serve a stale copy a moment longer.
6.2 Choosing a TTL is a real trade-off
blocks.text: 6.2 Choosing a TTL is a real trade-off

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281173736-7427438.png
blocks.alt: A short TTL keeps content fresh but generates more origin traffic; a long TTL is efficient but slower to reflect changes

blocks.content: There is no universally correct TTL, only a trade-off tuned to what the content actually is. An image that never changes once uploaded can safely cache for a year. A homepage banner that changes with every marketing campaign needs a TTL measured in minutes, or needs to rely on active purging instead of waiting for time to pass at all.
7. Purging and Invalidation at the Edge
blocks.text: 7. Purging and Invalidation at the Edge

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281176184-75235075.png
blocks.alt: A fresh deployment triggers a purge request across every edge, forcing each one to fetch the new version on the next request

blocks.content: Sometimes content needs to change before its TTL naturally expires, a bug fix ships, a price on a product page updates, a deleted image needs to actually disappear. CDNs support explicit purging (also called invalidation) for exactly this: an API call tells every edge location worldwide to drop a specific cached file immediately, so the next request for it anywhere in the world becomes a fresh cache miss that pulls the corrected version from the origin.

This is the exact same cache invalidation problem covered in depth elsewhere in this section, just operating at global scale, across potentially hundreds of edge locations instead of one shared cache cluster.
7.1 Serving stale content on purpose
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281177948-472658565.png
blocks.alt: When the origin is down, serving a stale cached copy is often far better than showing an error to every single user

blocks.content: Counterintuitively, one of the most valuable CDN features is deliberately serving stale content under one specific condition: the origin is completely unreachable. Rather than every user worldwide seeing an error page the moment an origin server has an outage, a well-configured CDN keeps serving the last known-good cached copy until the origin recovers. A slightly outdated page is almost always a better user experience than no page at all.
8. CDNs for Dynamic Sites and Edge Compute
blocks.text: 8. CDNs for Dynamic Sites and Edge Compute

blocks.content: The newest generation of CDNs go beyond passively caching files, they let you run actual application logic at the edge itself, close to the user, rather than only ever forwarding uncacheable requests all the way back to a distant origin. This lets things like authentication checks, A/B test routing, or lightweight personalization happen at the edge in milliseconds, only falling back to the origin for the parts of a request that truly need it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028795-950750448.png
blocks.alt: Simple, cheap logic runs right at the edge; only requests that genuinely need the origin ever travel that far

blocks.content: Concretely, this looks like Cloudflare Workers or AWS Lambda@Edge, small functions that run on every edge server itself. A common pattern checks an auth cookie right at the edge and rejects invalid requests immediately, so an attacker probing for weaknesses never even reaches the origin infrastructure. Another common pattern routes users into different A/B test variants at the edge, so the origin application never has to implement that routing logic itself.
8.1 TLS termination at the edge
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281182088-961541792.png
blocks.alt: Encrypting and decrypting the connection at the nearest edge, rather than all the way back at the origin, shaves real time off every request

blocks.content: CDNs also commonly terminate TLS (the encryption handshake behind HTTPS) right at the edge, physically close to the user, rather than forcing that entire handshake to travel all the way to a distant origin server. This alone shaves meaningful time off every single request, encryption handshakes involve several network round trips, and each one benefits from happening over a short local hop instead of a long-distance one.
8.2 Compression at the edge
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028798-379202304.png
blocks.alt: Files get compressed once at the edge, then served in their smaller form to every subsequent request

blocks.content: Many CDNs also compress responses (gzip or the newer Brotli) automatically at the edge, shrinking the actual bytes that travel the final, and often slowest, leg of the journey to the user device.
9. Real-World CDNs

{"headers":["Provider","Known for"],"rows":[["Cloudflare","Massive edge network plus security features (DDoS protection, WAF) bundled in"],["Akamai","One of the oldest and largest CDNs, heavily used by major enterprises"],["Amazon CloudFront","Deep integration with the rest of AWS (S3 origins, Lambda@Edge)"],["Fastly","Known for very fast purge propagation and real-time configuration"]]}

Naming a specific provider and one thing it is genuinely known for tends to land better in an interview than a generic list, it signals real familiarity with the ecosystem rather than a memorized table.
9.1 Tiered CDN pricing and coverage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281186234-746859792.png
blocks.alt: A larger network with more edge locations typically costs more than a smaller, more limited one

blocks.content: CDN providers typically offer tiers with meaningfully different global coverage, a budget tier might have edge locations concentrated in North America and Europe, while a premium tier covers dozens of countries across every continent. Choosing a tier is really a question about where your actual users are, paying for global coverage nobody in Southeast Asia will ever use is money spent solving a problem you do not have.
10. When a CDN Is Not Enough
blocks.text: 10. When a CDN Is Not Enough

blocks.content: ["Highly personalized, rarely-repeated responses gain little from edge caching, there is nothing to reuse.","Write-heavy operations cannot be served by a CDN at all, a CDN accelerates reads, it does not help you write data faster.","Extremely fresh, real-time data (a live stock price, a live sports score) may need TTLs so short that caching barely helps, and a different approach, like the realtime update patterns covered elsewhere, is a better fit."]
items: Highly personalized, rarely-repeated responses gain little from edge caching, there is nothing to reuse.
Write-heavy operations cannot be served by a CDN at all, a CDN accelerates reads, it does not help you write data faster.

Extremely fresh, real-time data (a live stock price, a live sports score) may need TTLs so short that caching barely helps, and a different approach, like the realtime update patterns covered elsewhere, is a better fit.

blocks.title: A useful mental test
blocks.content: Ask whether the exact same bytes would be correct for the next thousand people who request this URL. If yes, a CDN helps enormously. If the answer depends on who is asking, a CDN alone will not solve the problem, and may actively cause bugs if configured carelessly.
11. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 11. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a CDN comes up in an interview, the strongest answers connect it back to first principles rather than just naming vendors: a CDN exists because physical distance costs latency, and the fix is moving a cached copy of the data physically closer to the user. From there, being able to speak to origin pull versus push, what is and is not safe to cache, and how purging works, shows a real understanding rather than a memorized definition.
A CDN is caching applied at the scale of the entire internet, not a separate concept from caching.

A strong closing point in an interview is naming the specific latency number a CDN improves, roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds saved for a cross-continent user, since concrete numbers consistently land better than an abstract claim that a CDN simply makes things faster.
Key Takeaways

["A CDN solves latency caused by physical distance by serving cached content from an edge location near the user instead of a single distant origin.","Anycast or DNS-based routing sends each user to their nearest edge automatically, invisibly to the application.","Origin pull caches content lazily on first request; origin push proactively uploads content ahead of demand.","Cache-Control headers from the origin tell every edge exactly how long content can be reused.","Purging lets content be invalidated across every edge immediately, without waiting for a TTL to expire.","Highly personalized, write-heavy, or truly real-time data gets little benefit from a CDN."]
items: A CDN solves latency caused by physical distance by serving cached content from an edge location near the user instead of a single distant origin.
Anycast or DNS-based routing sends each user to their nearest edge automatically, invisibly to the application.
Origin pull caches content lazily on first request; origin push proactively uploads content ahead of demand.
Cache-Control headers from the origin tell every edge exactly how long content can be reused.
Purging lets content be invalidated across every edge immediately, without waiting for a TTL to expire.
Highly personalized, write-heavy, or truly real-time data gets little benefit from a CDN.

blocks.content: This topic connects closely to two others in this course: Cache Invalidation, since purging a CDN edge is the exact same problem at global scale, and Cache Consistency, since a CDN cache is, in the end, just another layer where the question "how stale is too stale" has to be answered explicitly.
A useful way to internalize this whole topic: a CDN is what caching looks like once you stop thinking at the scale of one data center and start thinking at the scale of the entire planet.
